Thales of Miletus. Around six hundred and twenty-four to five hundred and forty-six BCE, he was an early Ionian Greek philosopher credited with founding Western natural philosophy. He asked the most basic question: what is the fundamental substance of the universe? And he proposed that water was the primal element from which all things arise. He introduced mathematics and astronomy to the Greeks, and by Aristotle's account, he was the first philosopher.

Thales was born in Miletus, an Ionian Greek city in what is now Turkey, during an era of political upheaval. No writings of his survive. What we know about him comes from Aristotle, Herodotus, and later sources. Aristotle credits him as the founder of natural philosophy, which he called physika—the inquiry into the nature of things. He traveled to Egypt and Babylon, and it was said that he introduced geometry and astronomy to Greece.

His reasoning about water was simple but revolutionary. All life depends on moisture. Seeds are moist. Decay is the process of drying out. Water seems primordial. Every living thing, he argued, arises from water and returns to water. Heat and cold are merely modifications of moist matter. This was natural philosophy, not myth. He explained things through physical process, not divine will.

He extended this naturalistic approach to other phenomena. Eclipses, he said, happen because the moon blocks the sun. Not divine intervention—just mechanics. He allegedly predicted a solar eclipse, possibly the eclipse of five hundred and eighty-five BCE, though historians still dispute whether this claim is true. He introduced mathematics to Greece and applied geometry to practical problems like measuring heights and distances. He advocated clear thinking and observation, not revelation or poetry.

Thales founded what became the Milesian school, continued by Anaximander and Anaximenes. All three sought a single primal substance. His work marked the shift from mythological to physical explanation, and that shift defines the birth of Western science. His claim that water is fundamental turned out to be false, but his method—seeking a unifying physical principle—became the foundation of physics.
